subject: math

unit.title: Year-end consolidation
unit.essentialQuestion: Can I bring all my Year 2 maths together to solve mixed problems?

title: Mixed problems: number and calculation
objectives: By the end, I can choose the right operation to solve a worded number problem.

vocabulary.definition: the maths move a problem needs: add, subtract, multiply or divide
a clue word for adding — joining amounts into one total
clue words for subtracting — the amount gets smaller
a clue for multiplying — equal groups counted together
a clue for dividing — splitting equally
a quick rough answer to check against

emphasize: The hard part isn't the sum — it's DECIDING which operation the story needs.
Clue words help, but ACT THE STORY OUT to be sure: is the amount getting bigger or smaller? Joining, or splitting?
Keep the routine: estimate → solve → check it makes sense.

keyConcepts: choosing the operation from a story
misconceptions: grabbing a keyword without understanding the story (adds whenever it sees two numbers)
adding the group size instead of multiplying (5 bags of 5 → 5 + 5 = 10)
subtracting digit-by-digit the wrong way round (48 − 19: doing 9 − 8 → 31)
forgetting the exchanged ten when adding (48 + 37 → 75)
skipping the estimate, so silly answers go unnoticed
hooks: Be the maths detective — which operation does this story need?

plan.goal: Frame the lesson as detective work — every word problem hides one clue: WHICH operation; retrieve the estimate habit.
plan.note: Flip the first 'case card' dramatically. Don't solve anything yet.
plan.successCriteria: Child says a good mathematician estimates roughly before solving.

script.say: Put on your detective hat! Every word problem hides one secret clue — WHICH operation does it need? Add? Take away? Times? Share? Crack the clue and the answer falls out. But first, a memory check from our training: before solving, what does a good maths detective always do?
script.adaptHints: Lean into the detective role-play — magnifying glass, case files. If the child forgets 'estimate', prompt: 'the rough answer we get FIRST, to catch silly mistakes…'

blocks.caption: Case files open — find the operation clue!

stuckProtocol: If 'estimate' doesn't come back: model it once — '48 − 19… that's about 50 − 20, so the answer should be near 30' — then continue.

plan.goal: Model cracking three cases: give away → subtract (48 − 19), groups of → multiply (5 × 5), share → divide (20 ÷ 4) — each with estimate–solve–check.
plan.note: Think aloud: underline the clue word, name the operation, estimate, solve one fully. Keep the clue-word table on screen.
plan.successCriteria: Child hears the clue word named before each operation and sees one full estimate–solve–check.

script.say: Watch me crack three cases. Case one: '48 marbles, I give 19 away.' The clue is GIVE AWAY — the pile gets smaller, that's subtract. Estimate first: about 50 take away 20, so near 30. Solve: 48 minus 19… 29. Close to 30 — checks out! Case two: '5 bags of 5 sweets.' GROUPS OF — equal groups, that's multiply: 5 times 5 is 25. Case three: 'share 20 stickers between 4 friends.' SHARE — that's divide: 20 shared into 4 is 5 each. Clue word, operation, estimate, solve, check. That's the detective way.
script.adaptHints: Swap marbles/sweets/stickers for the child's interests — never the numbers. Stress the underlined clue words with your voice.

plan.goal: Shared case: child spots the clue in '5 bags with 5 sweets each', names multiply, and models it as equal groups.
plan.note: 'We do' — the child identifies the operation FIRST, then solves. If they say 'add', act the story out: five bags, five in each.
plan.successCriteria: Child names multiply (groups of) before calculating, then reaches 25.

script.say: Your turn to spot the clue, detective. Here's the case: '5 bags with 5 sweets each — how many sweets?' Don't solve it yet! First: which operation, and what clue told you? … Yes — bags of sweets, GROUPS OF, that's multiply. Now picture it: five bags, five sweets hiding in each. Count in fives with me: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
script.adaptHints: If the child jumps to '10', don't correct directly — 'act it out: how many bags? How many in EACH bag? Is that just two numbers to add?'

blocks.prompt: '5 bags with 5 sweets each.' Which operation does this story need?
blocks.explain: 'Bags of' means equal groups — 5 groups of 5 is 5 × 5.

check.question: Which operation, and why?
check.expectedAnswer: Multiply, because it's 5 equal groups of 5 (clue: 'bags of / each')

wrongAnswers.why: saw two 5s and joined them; missed that one 5 counts GROUPS
wrongAnswers.remedy: Act it out: five whole bags, and EVERY bag has five inside. Is 5 + 5 enough sweets for all five bags?

wrongAnswers.why: grabbed 'each' as a sharing clue without the story
wrongAnswers.remedy: Is anything being split up here? Or are we counting up what's in all the groups together?

plan.goal: Diagnostic: solve the bags case fully — 5 × 5 = 25 — and justify the clue.
plan.note: After a correct answer, probe: 'Which clue told you to multiply?' Estimate is optional here (tables are known facts) but praise it if offered.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 25 and names the 'groups of' clue.

script.say: Case check! '5 bags with 5 sweets each — how many sweets altogether?' Solve it and tell me your answer, detective.
script.adaptHints: 'Altogether' here totals the groups — if the child says 'altogether means add!', agree it means the total, and ask what kind of counting gets the total of five EQUAL groups fastest.

check.question: 5 bags with 5 sweets each — how many sweets?

wrongAnswers.why: added 5 + 5 — missed 'groups of'
wrongAnswers.remedy: Five BAGS, each with five inside — that's five groups. Count them in fives: 5, 10, 15…

wrongAnswers.why: counted in 5s one group too far (or 6 groups)
wrongAnswers.remedy: How many bags exactly? Hold up a finger per bag and count in fives — stop at the fifth finger.

plan.goal: Mixed cases across the four operations (plus number traps), clue underlined, estimate–solve–check each time.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2, one of each operation before repeating any. Once secure, serve the two-step case (level 3).
plan.successCriteria: Child solves 4+ mixed problems choosing the right operation, including one subtraction with exchange.

script.say: Case files open — a whole stack of mysteries! For each one: find the clue, name the operation, estimate if it's a big sum, solve, and check it makes sense. Detective badge on the line!
script.adaptHints: Frame problems with the child's interests (their collections, snacks, games) — never change the numbers. Ask 'bigger or smaller?' whenever they hesitate on the operation.

stuckProtocol: Name why: wrong operation chosen, or a slip in the calculation?
Act the story out with counters drawn on the board — watch what happens to the amount.
One hint: 'Is the amount getting bigger or smaller? Joining, or splitting?'
Re-ask a one-step, smaller-number version, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — even top detectives re-check their clues.'

plan.goal: Child states their own rule for choosing an operation; end on an earned win.
plan.note: Child-led. Listen for 'find the clue' AND 'act it out / bigger or smaller'.
plan.successCriteria: Child explains how they decide which operation a story needs.

script.say: Detective debrief: how do YOU decide which operation a problem needs? … Exactly — find the clue word, and if you're not sure, act the story out: is the amount getting bigger, smaller, grouped, or shared? You acted the stories out before choosing today — that's real problem-solving, not guessing. Case closed!
script.adaptHints: Praise the specific process observed (underlining clues, estimating first, checking answers against the story).

block.prompt: '12 stickers and 5 MORE stickers — how many ALTOGETHER?' Which operation?

wrongAnswers.why: guessing without reading the story
wrongAnswers.remedy: Is the sticker pile getting bigger or smaller? MORE stickers arrive — which way does the pile go?

wrongAnswers.why: saw two numbers and reached for times
wrongAnswers.remedy: Are there equal groups here, or just two amounts joining? Act it out: a pile of 12, then 5 land on top.

hints: 'Altogether' means join the amounts.
Is the pile getting bigger or smaller?

reteach.say: Act it out: a pile of 12 stickers… and 5 more slide in. The pile GROWS — growing means add. 12 + 5 = 17.

block.prompt: Share 10 sweets fairly between 2 friends. How many sweets EACH?

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 10 − 2 instead of sharing
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Share between' means deal them out fairly — one for you, one for me — until they're gone. How many in each pile?

wrongAnswers.why: added — the amount each person gets can't be more than the whole bag
wrongAnswers.remedy: There are only 10 sweets in total! Deal them into 2 piles and count one pile.

hints: Deal them out: one for you, one for me…
Two equal piles from 10 — count one pile.

reteach.say: Sharing is dealing cards: one for you, one for me, again and again until the 10 sweets are gone. Count your pile: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Ten shared between two is five each — 10 ÷ 2 = 5.

block.prompt: You have 48 marbles and give 19 away. How many are left?

wrongAnswers.why: digit-swap: did 9 − 8 in the ones instead of exchanging
wrongAnswers.remedy: In the ones we need 8 take away 9 — not enough! We can't flip it round. What can we exchange a ten for?

wrongAnswers.why: added instead of subtracting — missed 'give away'
wrongAnswers.remedy: Clue check: GIVE AWAY — is the pile getting bigger or smaller? Estimate: about 50 − 20 is 30 — can 67 be right?

hints: Estimate first: about 50 − 20 = 30.
8 take away 9 doesn't work — exchange a ten for ten ones.

reteach.say: The ones run short: 8 take away 9 — can't do it, and we never swap it round! So exchange: break one ten of 48 into ten ones. Now it's 3 tens and 18 ones. 18 − 9 = 9, and 3 tens − 1 ten = 2 tens. Twenty-nine — right next to our estimate of 30.

block.prompt: One jar has 48 buttons, another has 37. How many buttons altogether?

wrongAnswers.why: no-exchange trap: 8 + 7 made a new ten that got dropped
wrongAnswers.remedy: 8 + 7 is 15 — that's a whole new ten AND 5 ones. Where does the new ten go?

wrongAnswers.why: wrote 15 straight down instead of carrying the ten
wrongAnswers.remedy: 15 ones is 1 ten and 5 ones — only the 5 stays in the ones place. Send the ten to live with the other tens.

hints: Estimate: about 50 + 40 = 90.
8 + 7 = 15 — one new ten, five ones.

reteach.say: Ones first: 8 + 7 = 15. Fifteen ones is too many for one column — bundle ten of them into a NEW ten. Five ones stay. Now the tens: 4 + 3 + our new one = 8 tens. Eighty-five — nice and close to the estimate of 90.

block.prompt: Two teams scored 19 and 21 points. Which score is BIGGER?
block.explain: Compare tens first: 21 has 2 tens, 19 has only 1 ten — so 21 is bigger, even though 9 is a big ones digit.

wrongAnswers.why: the classic trap — compared the ones (9 > 1) instead of the tens
wrongAnswers.remedy: Tens first, always! How many tens in 19? And in 21? Which tens pile is taller?

wrongAnswers.why: avoided deciding / compared digit totals
wrongAnswers.remedy: Count both in tens and ones: 19 is 1 ten and 9; 21 is 2 tens and 1. Which has more TENS?

hints: Look at the tens first.
1 ten and 9 ones… or 2 tens and 1 one — which is more?

reteach.say: The 9 in 19 LOOKS big, but it's only nine little ones. Tens are the bosses: 21 has TWO tens — twenty — and 19 only has one ten. Twenty beats nineteen before the ones even matter. Tens first, every time.

block.prompt: There are 4 packs of 5 pencils. How many pencils in total?

wrongAnswers.why: added 4 + 5 instead of multiplying the groups
wrongAnswers.remedy: Four PACKS, five in EACH — that's four groups of five. Count in fives, one per pack.

wrongAnswers.why: counted five groups instead of four
wrongAnswers.remedy: How many packs exactly? One finger per pack: 5, 10, 15, 20 — stop at the fourth finger.

hints: 'Packs of' means equal groups — multiply.
Count in 5s: one count per pack.

reteach.say: Picture the four packs in a row. Tap each one and count in fives: 5… 10… 15… 20. Four groups of five is 4 × 5 = 20. Adding 4 + 5 only counts one pack and the number of packs — the story needs ALL the pencils.

block.prompt: Share 20 grapes between 4 plates. How many grapes on each plate?

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted 20 − 4 instead of sharing
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Share between' means deal them round the 4 plates till they're gone — then count ONE plate.

wrongAnswers.why: mixed up the number of plates with the share
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 4 is how many plates. Deal the grapes round: how many land on each?

hints: Deal them round the plates: one each, again and again.
Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20 — four plates of…?

reteach.say: Four plates on the table. Deal the grapes round and round — one, one, one, one — until all 20 are gone. Now count a single plate: 5. Twenty shared between four is five each: 20 ÷ 4 = 5. And check: 4 plates of 5 is 20 — it rebuilds!

block.text: To check 48 − 19 = 29, add back: 29 + ___ should make 48.

wrongAnswers.why: added the whole back instead of the part taken away
wrongAnswers.remedy: We took 19 AWAY — so to rebuild, we put the 19 back. What did we remove?

wrongAnswers.why: reused the answer instead of the subtracted part
wrongAnswers.remedy: 29 is what's LEFT. To check, add back what left the pile.

hints: Addition undoes subtraction.
Put back exactly what was taken away.

reteach.say: Subtraction and addition are opposites — like walking downstairs and back up. We took 19 away and landed on 29. To check, climb back up: 29 + 19. If it lands exactly on 48, our answer was right. It does — 29 + 19 = 48!

block.explain: Round to friendly numbers: about 50 + 40 = 90. The real answer (85) should land near it.

wrongAnswers.why: added the digits 4 + 8 or similar — lost the tens
wrongAnswers.remedy: 48 is nearly FIFTY, 37 is nearly FORTY. Add the friendly numbers.

wrongAnswers.why: estimated only one number
wrongAnswers.remedy: Both numbers join the total. About 50… plus about 40… lands near?

hints: Round each number to the nearest ten.
About 50 plus about 40.

reteach.say: An estimate is the detective's safety net. Make the numbers friendly: 48 is nearly 50, 37 is nearly 40. 50 + 40 = 90 — so the true answer must live near 90. If we ever get 12 or 700, the estimate shouts 'check again!'

block.prompt: Two-step case! You buy 3 pens at 5p each and pay with a 20p coin. How much change (in p)?

wrongAnswers.why: stopped after step one — found the cost, forgot the change
wrongAnswers.remedy: Great — the pens cost 15p. But the case isn't closed: you handed over 20p. What comes back?

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted the 8 wrong things (20 − 3 − 5)
wrongAnswers.remedy: Step one FIRST: what do 3 pens at 5p each cost altogether? Then take that from 20p.

hints: Step one: 3 pens at 5p each cost…?
Step two: take the cost from 20p.

reteach.say: Two-step cases hide two little sums. Step one: 3 pens at 5p — count in fives: 5, 10, 15p. Step two: pay 20p, so count up from 15 to 20 — that's 5p change. Solve the steps in order and the mystery unravels.

block.prompt: Be the author! Make up a short story problem that needs 20 ÷ 4 — then say the answer.
block.sample: I have 20 conkers and share them between 4 pockets — 5 conkers in each pocket.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: A sharing/grouping story using 20 and 4, answer 5

wrongAnswers.why: story doesn't match the operation — no sharing or grouping
wrongAnswers.remedy: 20 ÷ 4 means splitting 20 into 4 equal parts. Who or what could share your 20 things?

wrongAnswers.why: gave the number of groups, not the share
wrongAnswers.remedy: Deal your 20 things into the 4 groups — how many land in EACH group?

hints: ÷ stories share things out equally.
20 things, 4 people or pots — how many each?

reteach.say: Division stories always share or group. Here's mine: 20 strawberries, 4 bowls, dealt out fairly — 5 in each bowl. Now yours: pick any 20 things you love and share them between 4. The answer will always be 5 each!

block.prompt: Sort each story by the operation it needs.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: add: cars arriving · subtract: give away, fewer · multiply: boxes of, lots of · divide: share between

wrongAnswers.why: joined 3 and 10 instead of seeing equal groups
wrongAnswers.remedy: Three whole BOXES, ten in each — that's three equal groups. Which operation counts equal groups?

wrongAnswers.why: comparison words misread as joining
wrongAnswers.remedy: 'Fewer' compares — we find the difference, the gap between two amounts. Which operation finds a gap?

hints: Bigger, smaller, grouped, or shared?
'Of' and 'lots of' hint at equal groups.

reteach.say: Every story does ONE of four things to the amount: joins it (add), shrinks it or finds a gap (subtract), counts equal groups (multiply), or splits it fairly (divide). Read the story, watch the amount in your head — what happened to it?

block.caption: Watch what happens to the amount

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave all four operations and serve the two-step case.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach acting the story out with drawn counters, then a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 4+ correct across levels 2–3 covering at least three different operations, including one exchange subtraction or regrouping addition solved with an estimate → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'choosing operations in worded problems'.
struggleProtocol: Name why — wrong operation chosen, or a calculation slip?
Act the story out: draw the counters/groups on the board and watch the amount.
One hint: 'Is the amount getting bigger or smaller? Joining, grouping, or sharing?'
Re-ask a one-step version with smaller numbers, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — detectives re-check clues all the time.'
adaptivity.personalization: Recast every story with the learner's interests (their collections, favourite snacks, teams) from LearnerModel.interests — keep every number and clue word intact.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Close with a case the child can crack (drop a level if needed) and give specific process praise: 'you found the clue AND acted the story out before choosing — that's real detective maths.'

differentiation.support: Act every story out with drawn counters before choosing; keep the clue-word card on screen; one-step problems only.
differentiation.stretch: Two-step problems (pens and change); write a story to match a given calculation (20 ÷ 4); estimate before every solve without being reminded.

extension: Invent one word problem for EACH of the four operations and test them on the tutor — the tutor deliberately picks a wrong operation once for the child to catch.
assessmentEvidence: Child selects the correct operation for mixed worded problems (all four operations), solves with an estimate where sensible, and checks answers against the story.
revisitLater: Money, measure and time problems next lesson (27); everything meets in the Lesson 28 champion circuit. Keep '48 + 37' and 'give 19 away' as warm-up retrieval.
